idea: Like maximum sum, but a negative number flips the biggest product into the smallest and vice versa. So track both the largest and the smallest product ending here.
pattern: Kadane variant tracking max and min
analogy: A seesaw: multiplying by a negative tips the heaviest side up to the top. The most negative product so far can become the biggest after one more negative.

computeWithDP.summary: Keep maxSoFar and minSoFar for subarrays ending at each index.
steps: Start max, min and result at nums[0].
For each num, the new max is the largest of num, max × num and min × num; the new min is the smallest of the same three.
Compute both from the old values (tempMax) before overwriting.

computeWithTwoPasses.summary: Scan left to right and right to left, multiplying a running product and resetting after zeros.
steps: Left to right: multiply into product, record the max, reset product to 1 after a zero.
Do the same right to left.
With an odd number of negatives, the best product drops either the first or the last negative; one of the two scans finds it.

computeWithBruteForce.summary: Every start, extend the end, keep the running product.
steps: For each i, multiply elements j ≥ i one at a time.
computeWithBruteForce.timeWhy: n starts × up to n ends.

computeWithRecursion.summary: The max/min idea, passing the running values through recursive calls.
steps: maxProductRecursive carries currentMax, currentMin and globalMax to the next index.
Each call computes the new max/min with the next number, the same way as the DP version.
It stops at the last index and returns globalMax.

pitfalls: Overwriting max before computing min with the old max.
Zeros: both methods restart naturally (num alone beats 0 × anything).
interview: Start from Maximum Subarray and say what changes: negatives flip order, so keep the min as well.
The two-pass trick is a nice alternative to mention if you've explained the main one.
